summary:
Nayarit is one of Mexico's 32 states and operates inside the national equality framework, which Human Rights Watch described as advancing but uneven in its report of 31 March 2025. That roundup counts 22 of the 32 states as having legislated an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, eight with no such procedure, and two that recognise recognition in practice without legislation. The same document records 2019 guidelines from the national Supreme Court on the subject and notes that only seven states extend recognition to children.

Nayarit is among the states with a statutory route. A 2017 reform of the state Civil Code established an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, allowing adults to change identity documents to match their gender identity. The inventory does not document how that procedure is applied in practice, nor whether Nayarit is among the seven states extending recognition to minors.

Nayarit is the first of Mexico's 32 states to criminalise transfemicide, introducing sentences of up to 60 years in 2024. Mexico City followed in July 2024 as the second jurisdiction to do so, with sentences of up to 70 years under the Paola Buenrostro law, named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished. That statute also allows friends, not only relatives, to identify and claim bodies and to drive investigations, a provision aimed at cases in which families disown trans relatives.

Protection on paper sits against entrenched impunity. In 2022 more than 95% of homicides in Mexico went unpunished, a rate believed to be higher for transfemicides. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP of 22 November 2024 concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice.

Trans-specific killings are recorded at scale. Transgender Europe's monitoring counts 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021 and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to the 100 recorded in another country of the region. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, with the killings drawing LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests; Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months.

Where recognition is delayed or refused, documents contradict lived identity and compound everyday exposure. Human Rights Watch's report of 6 March 2024 found that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying such documents, amplifying discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police; the same report set those barriers against killings, including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023. Partnership recognition is settled nationally: same-sex marriage has been legal since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.
tangentialFactors:
Impunity shapes the practical value of Nayarit's transfemicide statute. With more than 95% of homicides in Mexico going unpunished in 2022 and rates for transfemicides believed to be worse, a sentence of up to 60 years describes an outcome that most families of victims never reach.

The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights has treated violence against trans people in Mexico as a regional concern, pressing federal and state authorities in 2024 for prevention and investigation that respects gender identity.

Comparative monitoring places Mexico among the countries with the highest recorded transfemicide totals, second for the year to September 2023 behind a country recording 100 against Mexico's 52.

The gap between statute and practice is the recurring finding of independent analysis. Beer's work for the LSE USAPP concludes that progressive legislation is rarely enforced uniformly, and cautions that formal rights must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not show how Nayarit's 2017 recognition procedure is applied in practice, including processing times, refusals, or whether applicants encounter administrative obstruction.

Whether Nayarit is one of the seven states extending legal gender recognition to children is unresolved in the sources provided.

No source in the inventory records a prosecution, conviction or sentence under Nayarit's 2024 transfemicide statute, so its enforcement record is not sourced here.

It is unresolved whether Nayarit's transfemicide law includes a provision comparable to the Mexico City statute's provision on identification and claiming of bodies by friends.

The sources do not state Nayarit's own homicide or transfemicide clearance rates; the national figure of more than 95% of homicides unpunished in 2022 is the only quantified measure available.

Whether the 2019 national Supreme Court guidelines have been applied by Nayarit authorities, and how Nayarit's procedure interacts with federal document rules at borders and airports, is not covered by the inventory.
